titleStmt.title: Be American and The Lonesome Mermaid
titleStmt.author: Carlos Bulosan

publicationStmt.p: These are transcriptions and encoded versions of 'Be American' and 'The Lonesome Mermaid' by Carlos Bulosan. These stories have been transcribed with readablity in mind with the orginal page breaks preserved. Spelling errors have also been preseved along side corrections.

sourceDesc.p: Transcribed from papers kept by Bulsan that are now held in UW Special Collections. The files used were originally typed on a typewriter and feature handmade corrections by the author.

'Be American' and 'The Lonesome Mermaid' are short stories by Filipino-American author and poet, Carlos Bulosan. 'Be American' tells the story of a narrator trying to help his cousin (a Filipino immigrant) adjust to live in the US.'The Lonesome Mermaid' is a fantasy following a child (presumably in the Philippines) who observes a strange man in his village who claims to be in love with a mermaid who has been kidnapping promising young men.

editorialDecl.p: We have decided to correct Bulosan's spelling errors but have included notes stating when these changes were made. We have also done this when the text was smudged or illegible.

body.p: It was not Consorcio’s fault. My cousin was an illiterate peasant from the vast plains of Luzon. When he came off the boat in San Francisco, he could neither read nor write English or Ilocano, our dialect. I met him when he arrived, and right away he had bright ideas in his head.

p.said: “Cousin, I want to be American,” he told me.
“Good,” I said. “That is the right thing to do. But you have plenty of time. You are planning to live permanently in the United States, are you not?”

body.p:
“Sure, cousin,” he said. “But I want to be American right away. On the boat I say, ‘Consorcio
stoody Engleesh will study English right away.’ Good ideeyas Good ideas , eh, cousin?”
“It is,” I said. “But the first thing for you to do is look for a job.”

p.said: “Sure, cousin. You have joob job for me?”

body.p:
I did. I took him to a countryman of ours who owned a small restaurant on Kearny Street. He had not done any dishwashing in the Philippines, so he broke a few dishes before he realized that the dishes were not coconut shells that he could flagrantly throw around the place, the way he used to do in his village where coconut shells were plates and carved trunks of trees were platters and his fingers were spoons. He had never seen bread and butter before, so he lost some weight before he realized that he had to eat these basic things like the rest of us, and be an American, which was his own idea in the first place. He had never slept in a bed with a mattress before, so he had to suf-
"Be American" 2 fer from severe cold before he realized that he had to sleep inside of the bed, under the blankets, but not on top of the spread, which was what we had done during his first two weeks in America. And of course he had never worn shoes before, so he had to suffer a few blisters on both feet before he realized that he had to walk light-footed, easy, and even graceful, but not the way he used to do it in his village, which was like wrestling with a carabao or goat.
All these natural things he had to learn during his first two weeks. But he talked about his Americanization with great confidence.
“You see, cousin,” he told me, “I have earned mony money quick. I poot and hoot dashes dishes in the sink, wash-wash, day come, day out, week gone - mony money ! Simple?”
“Fine,” I said.

p.said: “You know what I done with mony money ?”

body.p:
I went with him to his small room at the back of the restaurant where he was working, near the washrooms. And sure enough, he had lined the four walls of his room with big books. I looked at the titles. He had a cheap edition of the classics, books on science, law and mathematics. He even had some brochures on political and govern-mental matters. All were books that a student or even a professor would take time to read.
I turned to my cousin. He was smiling with pride.
“Well, I hope these big books will make you an American faster,” I told him.
“Five years?” There was genuine surprise in his dark peasant face. “Too long. I do not wait. I make faster - one year.”
“It is the law,” I assured him.

p.said: “No good law. One year enough for Consorcio. He make good American citizen.”
“There is nothing you can do about it.”

body.p: But he was puzzled. So I left him. I left San Francisco. When I saw him a year later, he was no longer washing dishes. But he still had the pardonable naivete of a peasant from the plains of Luzon.
“Where are you working now?” I asked him.
“Bakery,” he said. “I make da the bread. I make da donot the donut . I made da pys the pies .”

It was a small shop, a three-men affair. Consorcio was the handy-boy in the place, scrubbing the floor, washing the pots and pans; and he was also the messenger. The owner was the baker, while his wife was the saleswoman. My cousin lived at the back of the building, near the washrooms. He had a cot in the corner of a dark room. But the books were gone.
“What happened to your books?” I asked him.
He looked sad. Then he said, “I sold, cousin.”

p.said: "I cannot read. I cannot understand. Words too big and too long."
"You should begin with simple grammar books."
"Those cannot read also. What to do now, cousin?"
"You still want to be an American citizen?"

body.p:
"The school is free," I told him. "It is for foreign born people.
For adults, so they could study American history."

p.said:
"Well, work in the daytime. Look for another job. You still want
to be an American, don't you?"
"Sure. But I like boss-man. What to do?"

body.p:
I did. We went to the boss-man. I explained the matter as truth-
fully as I could and he understood Consorcio's problems.
But he asked me to find someone to take the place of my cousin's place, which I
did too, so we shook hands around and departed in the best of humor
I helped Consorcio register at the night school, looked for another
job for him as janitor in an apartment building. Then I left him,
wishing him the best of luck.
I worked in Alaska the next two years. When I returned to the mainland, I made it my duty to pass through San Francisco. But my
"Be American" 5 cousin had left his janitor job and the night school. I could not
find his new address, and it seemed that no one knew him well enough
in the Filipino community.

I did not think much of his disappearance because we are a wander-
ing people que to the nature of our lowly occupations, which take us
from place to place, following the seasons. When I received a box of
grapes from a friend, I knew he was working in
the grape fields in either Fresno or Delano, depending on the freight mark. When I re-
ceived a box of asparggus asparagus , I knew he was working in Stockton. But
when it was a crate of lettuce, he was working in Santa Maria or
Salinas, depending on the freight mark again. And in the summertime
when I received a large barrel of salmon, I knew he was working in
the salmon canneries inAlaska. There were no letters, no post cards
- nothing. But these surprising boxes, crates and barrels that arrived
periodically were the best letters in the world. What they contained
were lovingly distributed among my city friends. Similarly, when I
was in one of my own wanderings, which were done in cities and large
towns, I sent my friend or friends unsealed envelopes bursting with
the colored pictures of actresses and other beautiful women. I ad-
dressed these gifts to poolrooms and restaurants in towns where my
friends had lived or worked for a season, because they were bound to
go to any of these havens of the homeless wanderer. However, when
another curious wanderer opened the envelopes and pilfered the pic-
tures, it was not a crime. The enjoyment which was originally in-
tended for my friends was his and his friends. That is the law of the
nomad: finders keepers.

But Consorcio had not yet learned the unwritten law of the nomad.
I did not expect him to send me boxes, crates, and barrels from far-
away Alaska. So I did not know where I could locate him.

I wandered in and out of Los Angeles the next two years.
At the beginning of the third year, when I was talking to the sleeping birds
in Pershing Square, I felt a light hand on my shoulders. I was not
usually curious about hands, but it was well after midnight and the
cops were wandering in and out of the place. So I turned around
and jound found
Consorcio.

I found a new Consorcio. He had aged and the peasant naivete
was gone from his face. In his eyes was now a hidden fear. His hands
danced and flew when he was talking,
and even when he was not talking, as though he were slapping the wind with both hands or clapping with
one hand. Have you ever heard the noise of one hand clapping?

That was Consorcio, after five years in America. He was either
slapping the wind with both hands or clapping with one hand. So I
guided him out of the dark park to a lighted place, where we had cof-
fee until the city awoke to give us another day of hope. Of course,
I sat in silence for a long time because it was the year of deep si-
lence. And Consorcio sat for a long time too, because by now he had
learned to hide in the deep silence that was flung like a mourning
cloak across the face of the land. When we talked our sentences were
short and punctuated by long silences. So we conversed somewhat like this:

p.said: "Where have you been all these years?"

body.p: Silence.
Silence.

p.said: "Well, I could have told you. But I wanted you to learn."
"At least I speak better English now."
"This is a country of great opportunity."

body.p: Silence.

"You have a wonderful dream, cousin," he told me and left. He left
Los Angeles for a long time. Then, two years later, I received a crate
of oranges from him. The freight mark was San Jose. Now I knew he was
working and had learned the unwritten law of the wanderers on this
troubled earth. So as I ate the oranges, I recalled his last state-
ment: You have a wonderful dream, cousin…

I had a wonderful dream. But I dreamed it for both of us, for
many of us who wandered in silence. Then the boxes and crates became more frequent. Then a barrel of
salmon came from Alaska. And, finally, the letters came. My cousin
Consorcio, the one-time illiterate peasant from the vast plains of
Luzon, had indeed become an American without knowing it. He His letters
were full of wondering and pondering about many things in America.
Now he realized his naivete when he had landed in San Francisco. But
he realized also that he could not ask too much in a strange land.
And it was this realization that liberated him from his peasant pri-
"Be American" 8 son, his heritage, and eventually led him to a kind of work to which
he dedicated his time and life until the end.

I was in Oregon when I received a newspaper from Consorcio, post-
marked Pismo Beach. It was the first issue of his publication for
agricultural workers in California. It was in English. From then on,
I received all issues of his publication. All of the five years that
it existed depending defending the workers and upholding the rights and liberties
of all Americans, native or foreign born, so that, as he began to un-
derstand the nature of American society, he became more belligerent in
his editorials and had to go to jail a few times for his ideas about
freedom and peace.

Yes, indeed Corsorcio: you have become an American, a real Ameri-
can. And this land that we have known too well is not yet denuded by
the rapacity of men. Rolling like a beautiful woman with an overflow-
ing abundance of fecundity and murmurous with her eternal mystery,
there she lies before us like a great mother. To her we always return
from our prodigal wanderings and searchings for an anchorage in the
sea of life; from her we always draw our sustenance and noble thoughts,
to add to her glorious history.

But the war came. And the war ended Consorcio’s newspaper work
and his crusade for a better America. And it ended his life also.
When he was brought back from overseas, he knew he would not last long.
But he talked the way he had written his editorials, measured sentences
that range like music, great poetry, and soft, soft. He would not shed
a tear; but his heart must have been crying, seeing eternal darkness
coming toward him, deep, deep in the night of perpetual sleep. Yes,
he would not shed a tear; but he must have been crying, seeing that
there was so much to do with so little time left. There was in his
"Be American" 9 voice a kindness for me - unhappy, perhaps, that he could not impart
what he had learned from his wanderings on this earth : unhappy, also,
because he knew that it would take all the people to unmake the un-
happiness which had caught up with us. And now, fifteen years after
his arrival in San Francisco, he was dying.

And he died. But at least he received his most cherished dream:
American citizenship. He did realize later that he had become an
American before he received his papers, when he began to think and
write lovingly about our America. He gave up many things, and finally
his own life, to realize his dream.

But Consorcio is not truly dead. He lives in my undying
love for the American earth. And soon, when I see the last winter
coming to the last leaf, I will be warm with the thought that another
wanderer shall inherit the wonderful dream which my cousin and I had
dreamed and realized in America.

body.p:
Every once in a while the mermaid emerged from the depths of the river
when the moon was full and claimed her victims. She would appear among us
in the person of a beautiful young woman, then suddenly disappear with her
new young man. We often wondered why she always took with her the most
promising man in our town. We burned candles and chanted prayers when we
knew that the time had come when she would appear again.

But nobody actually saw her until a strange man came to live in our town.
Before his appearance we only noticed a strange and beautiful woman in our
religious processions, then the next day a promising young man with some beau-
ty would disappear forever. But the strange man who came to live in our town
finally gave us the reality of the mermaid’s existence and her traffic with
promising young men.

At first the men did not pay any particular attention to the stranger,
because he was always sitting under a mangotree in the yard. He was always
playing a homemade guitar. But the women looked out of their windows and
sighed with sympathy, because they thought the man was merely waiting for
the hour of death. As the years went by, however, the townspeople began to
forget him.

Then on evening toward the end of November, when we were harvesting
the highland rice in the south and or our field, the people began talking
ominously about the mermaid. Then my uncle came running with the starling
news that she would soon appear to claim her next victim.
“And this time, brother,” he vehemently to my father, “her victim is the stranger!”
“How do you know?” Father asked.

“The stranger himself said so,” he said. “That is why the whole town
is talking now.”

“Brother,” fathersaid quietly, as though he were humoring him, “you
have been living a shady life too long. You hear fantastic things, but per-
hapes it is because you have a guilty conscience.”

“Let’s run over to his house if you don’t believe me,” said my uncle.
“A big crowd is there watching him. And the mayor is asking him some strange
questions.”

“I’ve never seen a crazy man,” Fathercontemplated seriously. Then he
said to me. “Let’s go, son.”

We rushed to the stranger’s house. He was sitting under the mango tree
as usual, playing his homemade guitar. Then he got up and bowed courteous-
ly to us.
“What can I do for you, neighbors and friends?”he asked.

The mayor extricated himself from the crowd and approached the man.
“We have heard rumors about you and the mermaid that lives in the depths
of the river,” he said. But when the stranger did not answer, the mayor
said angerly. “Will you deny them to these people?”

“Why should I do that?” he said.“ The mermaid is in love with me, so
she is coming to take me!”

The old men stood in silence, their heads bowed low. The women dropped
on their knees and prayed.

The mayor became very angry. “How can you be very careless with words?”
he said. “But I will forget everything if you’ll now denay what you have
just said in .
so irreverent a manner. You are a Christian, ain’t you?”

“She is in love with me, that is all,”said the stranger. “Now tell me
this: is love the sole property of the human race?”

“I don’t know what you are talking about,” said the mayor. Then he said
to the people, “This man is a heretic! Let’s hang him!”

Slowly the stranger sat down and picked up his guitar. Delicately he
plucked at the strings, swaying from side to side. Then he stopped
and looked at us.

“The mermaid will appear tomorrow night,” he said distinctly, and his
voice echoed in the still night. “She will come for me. But you will not
see her because your hearts are impure. She shows herself only to the pure
of heart.”

“What are you saying?” demanded the mayor. “I wouldn’t have been elec-
ted if what you are implying is true.”
“And another election is approaching,”said the stranger.
“What, What?” shouted the mayor.

“But not only that,” explained the stranger. “You will not see her be-
cause your souls are corrupted. She shows herself only to the clean of soul.”
Then the mayor grabbed a piece of rope from a peasant. Father intervened.

“Wait,” Fathersaid, taking the rope from the mayor. “Why can’t we wait
until tomorrow night? We must give the man o a chance to prove his contention.
That is our way in these parts. Isn’t that so, Mayor?”

“All right,”said the mayor to the people. “We will give him another day.
Go home and sleep.”

There was a full moon the following night. The whole town was whisper-
ing and afraid. And the little boys and girls were locked in their houses.

Out in the presidencia yard the men were preparing a stout rope when a
runner came with the news that the stranger had just left his house.
“Was he trying to, escape?” asked the myaor mayor .

“He didn’t like he was in a hurry,” said the runner. “He was carrying
a fishing net and a lantern.”
“Did you see in what direction was he going?” Fatherasked.
“He was walking toward the river,” said the runner.

There was a deep silence for a minute. The men looked at each other for
a sign of action. Then the mayor ran across the yard and jumped on his horse.
And the other men followed him, riding at full speed through the silence of the
night.

Then I ran to my uncle’s house and woke him up. Then together we ran to
the river, where the sound of agitated men pierced the dark night.

“I have never seen a mermaid, nephew," shouted my uncle. “I’m glad you
woke me up. This is the night of all nights. I want you to remember it as
long as you live, because you might never see another mermaid again.”

“Maybe there are some mermaid running loose in the world,” I said. “I
understand you could see them walking in broad daylight in the big cities.”

“Those are mermaids of the land, nephew,” he said. “There are many of
them. But the one we are going to see is a mermaid of the water, and it is
not very often that we see them.”

“Maybe so,” I said. “I would like to see a mermaid, of the land or of
the water.”
“I would, too,”he said. “So let’s run like hell, nephew!”

We ran like hell. We found the mayorand the other men crouching behind
the tall reeds in the dry bottom of the river. The stranger was sitting at
the edge of the water on the opposite side of the river. The msmall small lantern
was flickering beside him.

But we could see him. The moon was full and bright. And the air was
very still. Suddenly, he blew out the lantern and thick clouds appeared
from somewhere and covered the moon. And the darkness that had descended
upon the world was so thick we had to join hands in order not to get lost.
And the river suddenly rose up violently, then ebbed away with a deadening
roar. When the moon came out the stranger was gone. THere there was only the
soft noise of the receding river and the vanishing phosphorescence of the
bright water. And an unidentified man conjectured about the stranger’s
disappearance.
“Maybe he jumped in the river and couldn’t swim,” said the mayor.
“Maybe he ran to the bushes on the other side of the river,” Fathersaid.
“Maybe he killed himself,” said my uncle.
“Lets look for his body,” suggested the mayor.

p.said: “There is no hurry,” said the runner.

body.p: “We will look for his body tomorrow,” said the mayor. “Poor man.”
No man was satisfied. But the crowd dispersed.

But in the morning, the body could not be found. The mayorsent several
divers to the bottom of the river, and they came up with a few bright peb-
bles and edible weeds and water plants. Then there were heated arguments
about the stranger’s disappearance. Some claimed that he had played a trick
on us, but the others thought that he was hiding somewhere in the rice fields
across the river. But we went home and forgot all about him.

Then many years passed. A war broke out somewhere and took most of the
young men away. And after thefaminedevastated our town. Then a
terrible plague came and destroyed almost everything alive. But a new ge-
neration grew up and laughed when they were told about the stranger and
the mysterious mermaid.

I was already a man when the stranger appeared again. I was wa lking on
our street when I met him by accident. And I could not believe my own eyes.
He was still a man of the same uncertain age, as though I were now the older
person.

“Are you thestranger who was supposed to have disappeared with the mer-
maid years ago?” I asked.

“Yes, son,” he said.“But I don’t remember seeing you around when I was
here.”

“It was a long time ago,” I said.“I was only a little boy when you went
away.”

“Have I been gone that long, son?”he asked. “We have no time under the
river."
“Did you really go away with the mermaid?” I asked.
“Yes,” he confessed. “I love her, and she loves me.”

“You are a lucky man,” I said. “I wish I were you. "I’m tired of living
in grass houses and working all day in the hot sun. And look how I am get-
ting old, while you are still the same age as when you left, if not younger.”

“That is human life,” he said. “We are born to do something, but the
arrangement of things in the world compels us to do what we are not fit for.
Some men are fortunate, others are not. Some become great leaders of men,
others become great lovers. But there are many degrees of greatness in seeking beauty,
and another greatness in knowing the truth. But the greatest greatness of all,
my son, is in seeking, sharing, giving love to one who seeks it and gives
it to another man as a token of living greatly and dying the same. I don’t
really know where you fit in the confused scheme of things, but I guess you
will find it in your time.”
“I am terribly afraid of the future,” I said.

“Life is a great adventure,”he said wisely. “Choose your own weapons
and your own hunting ground. I guess your luck will come somewhere on the
way.”
“I’ll keep on hoping,” I said. “And thank you for giving me courage.”

“Don’t despair, son,” he said. “It is not our doing that we are born
on this troubled earth. But it is not also our undoing that we must suffer
under these stars. Look now: it is not our individual lives that count in
the world. It is what goodness and beauty we contribute to life itself.
For my part, I have sacrificed my own life among men for a timeless one.
Yet I know that it is far better to have a crowded and useful transitory
life than a deathless one. Time, my son, I have seen the end of it.”
"I’ll remember everything,"I said.

“It is a timeless life,” he said dreamingly. “But I got lonesome for my
guitar. I’ve asked the queen, that is the mermaid, to get it back. I’m on
my way to my house now.”
“Your house is not there any more.” I said. “It disappeared years ago.”
“Did some man steal it?” he asked.

“It just rotted away with the years,” I said. “You have been gone a long
time. A war came and killed most of the young menbbefore men before my generation. Then a plague and a famine came after, killing the rest including my own generation. What you will see here are remnants of a one vigorous race. I don’t know what will happen to us in another generation.”

“My heart beats for you,” he said sadly.“But I’ve got to go now. The
queen will be disappointed when she hears that my guitar is gone.”

“I’ve a guitar,” I said. “I want to give it to you. I want you to be
happy with the queenin that timeless place.”

“Thank you, son,” he said. “You are very understanding and kind. I’ve
sacrificed my life for this town, but that is nothing. If I didn’t go with
the queen, she would have taken many of the young men in this town.”
“But why would she do that?” I asked.
“They wouldn't understand her,” he said,
“I would have understood her,” I said.

“I’m glad we understand each other,” he said. “I might want to live on
the earth again, and you could take my place.”
I remained silent.
“They wouldn’t have understood her,” he said again. “They are too human.”

"Thank you for your sacrifice,” I said. “Please give my best regards to
the queen.”

“Now, remember that mermaid are really kind and understanding,” he said.
“They are cruel sometimes because men don’t understand them. Men of the earth

p.said:
are always thinking of happiness in terms of happiness on the earth, Mer-
maids get lonesome, too.”

body.p: “I’ll always remember,” I said.

I watched him walked walk straight into the water. And the day became sud-
denly dark and murmurous. I heard the turbulent lashing and roaring of
the water in the momentary darkness. And when the sun came out the man was
gone, forever.

And the mermaid never came out of the secret depths again. Sometimes
the townspeople could hear the faraway sound of a guitar rising from the
river when the moon was full in the summer sky.
